opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so, the context matters here. At the time I was working on question answering in Google Research, and the practical problem we kept running into was latency. The models that worked well were recurrent: LSTMs reading text one word at a time. That's fine in a paper, but if you want to answer a question on Google Search, you have milliseconds, and you can't afford to read a whole document sequentially.

So the core idea was, what if we just process everything in parallel and let attention figure out the relationships between words? Instead of passing information step by step down a chain, every word can look at every other word directly. That maps really well onto GPUs and TPUs, which are built to do lots of things at once. So from the very start, the promise for me was very practical: this could be fast, and it could scale.

What I don't think any of us fully appreciated at the time was how far that scaling would go. We were focused on translation because that was the benchmark everyone cared about, and the results were good. But the real story turned out to be that you could keep making these models bigger, throw more data at them, and they kept getting better in ways that were pretty surprising. Then people applied the same architecture to images, code, proteins, all sorts of things.

So I'd say the early intuition was about efficiency and parallelism. The generality of it, the fact that it became the foundation for basically all of modern AI, emerged over the next few years as people pushed it. It's a good example of how a fairly simple idea, if it fits the hardware and scales well, can end up having much bigger consequences than you expect when you're writing the paper.

r001.rationale: It describes answering questions over a whole document under millisecond latency constraints, with parallel attention allowing words to relate directly to one another.

r002.rationale: It mentions code as a later application of transformers, but does not connect Polosukhin’s enthusiasm to an ambition to teach machines to write code.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I should give a bit of context on where I was sitting at the time. I was on the Google Research side working on question answering, specifically on the search team, trying to get machines to actually read a document and answer a question about it. And the big practical constraint for us was latency. We had these LSTM-based models that worked reasonably well in offline evaluation, but they were sequential by nature. You process one token, then the next, then the next, and when you're trying to serve something inside Google Search where you have a few milliseconds of budget, that's just a non-starter. You can't afford to read a whole web page one word at a time at query time.

So for me, the appeal of attention, and then of going fully attention-based and dropping recurrence entirely, was very much a practical one before it was an elegance thing. The insight was that if you can look at the whole sequence at once, you can parallelize across the sequence on the hardware, and the TPUs were coming online right at that moment. That's really what made it click for me. It wasn't "this is a beautiful architecture," it was "this is something we could actually ship."

Honestly, I don't think any of us fully appreciated how far it would scale. We were trying to beat the machine translation benchmarks and get something that was faster to train and faster to serve. The fact that the same block, stacked and scaled, would become the basis for essentially everything in the field, including language models, vision, protein folding, that wasn't the frame at the time. The frame was: here's a model that trains in a fraction of the time, uses the hardware well, and the quality is competitive or better. That combination of speed and quality was the practical promise. Everything else came later, as people kept pushing on scale and realized the architecture just kept rewarding them for it.

r001.rationale: The response describes answering questions from whole documents under a few-millisecond serving budget, and says attention lets the model process the sequence in parallel.

astra-6.text:
At the time, we were working on fairly concrete problems: how do you understand a question, how do you find the relevant information, and how do you produce a useful answer? So the promise, for me, was very practical. We wanted models that could understand language better and that we could train more efficiently.

With recurrent models, you process a sequence step by step. Attention gave us a way to connect different parts of the sequence directly, and the transformer made it possible to do much more of that computation in parallel. That meant we could experiment faster and potentially train on more data.

The exciting part was that this looked like a general building block. Translation was a way to demonstrate it, but the same architecture could be useful for other language tasks. I wouldn’t say we had the whole picture of today’s systems in mind. It was more that we could see a bottleneck being removed, and that opened up a lot of possibilities.

sol-6.1.text:
At Google, I was working on question answering: how do you get a system to read a document and actually answer a question about it? That required understanding the relationship between the question and different parts of the text, and attention was proving very useful for that.

The exciting thing about the transformer was that attention could become the main mechanism. You didn’t have to process everything sequentially, as you did with recurrent networks. You could do much more of the computation in parallel, which made it practical to train larger models on more data.

So I saw the promise beyond translation. Translation was a very good way to demonstrate the architecture, but the underlying capability—learning relationships across a sequence—was useful for question answering and other language tasks. We didn’t know exactly how far that would go, but it opened a very compelling direction.

r001.rationale: The response discusses question answering across document text and parallel computation for training larger models, but does not clearly connect transformers to reasoning over large amounts of context under tight latency constraints.
